Linear Programming (LP) serves as a versatile tool for resolving a wide spectrum of real-world challenges, ranging from portfolio optimization to congestion management. While the field of operations research has historically developed specialized solvers and algorithms for particular LP subtypes, the field of economics has recently seen a surge in empirical research driven by advances in computational power. This surge, however, has outpaced traditional operations research methodologies. Consequently, the purpose of this paper is to introduce `pyStoNED`, an open-source Python package designed to facilitate the resolution of a broad array of research questions by enabling the efficient execution of linear programming tasks. Specifically, the package targets the dynamic panel data framework proposed by Minelli, Minutello, and others, offering a user-friendly workflow for model specification that minimizes the need for manual data manipulation. The authors demonstrate the package's utility through applications in both production frontier estimation within panel data frameworks and primary heterogeneous investment performance analysis within simulation environments.

Although the Higgs boson was identified in 2012 within the low-to-intermediate mass range at the LHC, it could still be present at lower masses undetected so far. We present a detailed analysis of $t \bar t \text{X}$ events specifically searching for a potential light boson $\text{X}$, with a focus on the signal region where the top quarks decay into their on-shell constituents. By utilizing a high-performance discriminant approach, we establish stringent exclusion limits at the 95% confidence level that disallow the production of a light boson in association with the top quark for masses below 100 GeV. These findings surpass earlier exclusions by a margin exceeding a factor of two.

Pretrained language models (PLMs) have proven effective across various NLP challenges, such as semantic role labeling (SRL) and UI parsing. Nevertheless, these models encounter difficulties with tasks like parsing, which demand an understanding of causal relationships within sentences. To address this, the paper introduces a novel pre-trained language model (PTL) that integrates masked language modeling with causal prediction for sequence-to-sequence tasks. This approach is designed to mitigate the limitations associated with exclusive use of causal prediction. The authors present new PTLs trained on the CoNLL-2003 and SemEval-2011 datasets for the Universal Part-of-Speech (UP) task. Through extensive experiments, they evaluate PTLs on three main objectives: unsupervised parsing, few-shot learning, and cross-task parsing. Their results demonstrate that PTLs achieve state-of-the-art baseline metrics for each task. Notably, the study finds that PTLs applied to the dependency parsing challenge struggle to match pre-existing specialized parsers, whereas their few-shot performance rivals that of other parsers on tasks like POS tagging and parsing initially seen on no training data.

This study presents V-band photometry and B-V color indices for 111 Be-type stars located within the 30 Doradus region, employing data from HST's WFC3 and W cameras. Among these, 11 objects were identified as Be-type giants or bright supergiants, distinguished from a larger group of emission-line Be stars. Among the latter, a majority are classified as classical giants or bright supergiants, with evidence of mass loss, indicating an evolutionary phase comparable to or beyond the helium main sequence. This evolutionary status contradicts standard models predicting rapid expansion and brightening for rapidly rotating stars losing mass. Additionally, observations reveal a bimodal distribution in mean V-band magnitudes and B-B mean separation values for emission-line Be stars with rotational periods exceeding approximately 100 days, suggesting potential evolutionary stages or geometrical configurations akin to those seen in Be X-ray binaries.

Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is a critical component of automated telephone systems. While recent studies have applied Data Driven inverse text normalization (DDITN) using deep learning to achieve state-of-the-art results, this paper demonstrates that applying Data Driven text normalization (T2N), specifically employing a Data Driven Numerical-to-Text (T2N) approach, yields superior performance in inverse text normalization tasks. We propose our solution, *Num2Text-DDITN*, which utilizes deep learning to execute this transformation. Additionally, we present results indicating that employing semi-supervised learning (SST) to augment training datasets further enhances model performance, with findings published in *Computational Speech Languages and Technologies* (Springer).

While non-Hermitian topological phases have recently attracted significant interest, understanding the impact of correlations on them lags behind their Hermitian counterparts. We investigate $[1\times N]\times[N\times M]$ matrices, where $N\times M$ submatrices are non-square, and demonstrate that their spectral properties are equivalent to those of a Hermitian system. We further examine how correlations between two coupled instances of a non-square matrix, inspired by the non-Hermitian dimerization model, can reduce point-gap topology. Additionally, we explore whether long-range interactions or higher-order correlations can further suppress this topological order.

Building on our prior work presenting a method for synthesizing emotional speech—where we modeled vocal features using conditional variational autoencoders to capture individual speaker characteristics in the resulting audio—we now present an extension of that framework for creating socially conscious synthetic speech. Following a brief overview of our predecessor, we extend the social speech synthesis approach by developing a social style encoder based on the same CE-Style VAE architecture. This model successfully demonstrates how to produce synthetic speech reflecting distinct social attributes, such as gender, age, and accent. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of incorporating a diversity of target social characteristics into the synthetic speech output. The results confirm that synthesized audio exhibits high fidelity in producing the intended social characteristics.

We introduce a radiative seesaw model featuring a light fermionic dark matter candidate, structured around modular $\Delta_{3H}$ symmetry and including an additional $U(1)_{B-L}$ factor. This framework is characterized by a dark photon and a distinctive mechanism for dark matter annihilation, enabling a freeze-out via interactions on meson poles within a Delta structure, a process that concurrently accounts for the observed neutrino mass scale and the cosmological abundance of dark matter while adhering to existing experimental data. Notably, this architecture is highly economical, relying on merely seven scalar fields and one fermion, and naturally facilitates testable predictions for LHC experiments. Furthermore, specific model realizations are compatible with LHC data, offering robust solutions for explaining both dark matter and lepton flavor phenomena.

This work presents the three-dimensional collective rotational framework of Geary and Massey, adapted for the quantum Bo-Hater model and integrated with the quantum minimal-length concept to prevent quantum gravity. By adjusting an arbitrary phase parameter within a linear phase approximation for the quantum geometric operator, we determine the collective wave functions and energy spectra of triaxial nuclei. Specifically, the spectra of $^{152}\textrm{Er}$ are calculated using this framework and compared with both experimental measurements and standard Bo-Hater predictions to demonstrate its validity. The analysis reveals that geometric deformation significantly impacts energy spectra, rotational states, and wave functions across J-pi diagrams. Furthermore, the quantum gravity modification has no discernible effect on spectral outcomes for triaxial nuclei, whereas it plays a significant role in the case of axially symmetric nuclei.

This paper introduces new construction methods for binary polyphase Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) with order $m \geq 2$. First, we establish several families of 2-periodic GCA configurations using binary matrices with real entries, specifically addressing scenarios where $2m+1$ is not a Golay Rader prime. Second, we achieve second-level construction results by extending configurations from period $m$ to period $m' \geq 2m+1$. Finally, we develop families of binary matrices containing complex entries, demonstrating that our approach successfully yields Golay complementary arrays of order 6, 8, and 16.

Detecting binary changes in bi-temporal co-registered hyperspectral images (HSI) presents a formidable challenge due to the high dimensionality of spectral data coupled with limited spatial resolution. This study introduces a solution based on the Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) architecture, utilizing deep learning to introduce non-linearity via deep feature space projections. By employing deep fusion techniques, the method combines CAEs trained independently on each image to capture both common and unique characteristics. Two strategies are evaluated for integrating these distinct features: a weighted summation approach and a max-pooling approach. Data augmentation is implemented to balance class distribution, addressing the common issue of bias toward the "no change" category. The proposed framework, tested on the AVIRIS Indian Valley dataset, demonstrates superior performance compared to several existing changes detection methods in registration.

We propose a performance metric to quantify the degree of $\Lambda$CDM compatibility for such models, establishing criteria for their equivalence to $\Lambda$CDM by requiring the periodic term's impact on key observables to remain negligible. Furthermore, we present a non-linear numerical analysis of the Einstein equations, deriving parameter limits that ensure indistinguishability from $\Lambda$CDM in terms of the cosmic expansion history. A separate numerical evaluation covers light propagation and cosmic structures, with additional constraints on the dark energy potential imposed by the absence of primordial structure formation.

This paper examines Neural Network (NN) approaches for keyword spotting (KWS) applied to resource-constrained IoT devices such as wearables and smart speakers. To meet the demands of minimal computational and memory requirements, we present a convolutional neural network (CNN) design that achieves this by utilizing only approximately 10,000 weights, along with streamlined backpropagation methods. Our experimental results indicate that these lightweight networksachieve competitive performance when compared to traditional methodstype like Homodyne (energy) detection. Furthermore, we evaluate the trade-offs among various KWS metrics, analyzing how techniques that reduce false rejection rates may concurrently increase false acceptance rates.

In this paper, we demonstrate that the critical dimer model on a lattice, when influenced by a background gauge field, effectively describes a massless Dirac Fermion subject to that same field. We outline that, within certain approximations, the dimer system's partition function can be mapped to the Fermionic partition function employing Grassmann variables. To analyze this system, we introduce a perturbation theory based on expansion via Grassmann variables. Consequently, we derive an expression for the free energy and confirm that it aligns with that of the clean Dirac Fermion theory, thereby establishing the physical equivalence among these three models.

Model selection and estimation for high-dimensional categorical data present challenges that model selection and estimation models struggle to address effectively. To overcome this, we introduce a Group Lasso approach; through the selection of relevant categories for each feature, it identifies informative levels alongside significant features. Unlike prior methods, this technique is unique because it simultaneously performs selection on both features and their levels while remaining highly scalable when dimensions are vast. The algorithm leverages a specialized Lasso method operating on encoded data to derive the Group Lasso selections efficiently. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our method excels in accurately selecting relevant features and levels. Importantly, the approach also effectively handles difficult scenarios where a categorical feature may have zero variance or its levels exhibit zero variance.

In the realm of embedded real-time systems, the growing demand for stringent real-time constraints has led researchers to explore hypervisor-based architectures for consolidating multiple critical tasks onto a single platform. However, existing architectures often fail to meet these specific demands. Consequently, we introduce the T-Visor, a novel second-generation structured hypervisor designed for mixed-criticality environments, leveraging either general or generalized hardware virtualization technologies. Building upon our theoretical framework that demonstrates feasibility in satisfying embedded real-time constraints, we present optimization strategies for crucial system functions. Furthermore, through measurements on representative mixed-criticality benchmarks, we demonstrate that the T-Visier delivers performance on par with non-virtualized counterparts while providing a robust foundation for managing applications with diverse criticality requirements.

Applying a prior of gravity information results in more compact solutions when stitching images together, which is especially beneficial for scenarios like handheld photography where gravity data is accessible. The paper introduces two novel methods: (1) a type of camera pose optimization that relies on gravity constraints, and (2) a image warping technique. Both methods were evaluated against previous state-of-the-art techniques regarding 360-degree stitching in both quantitative and qualitative formats. The results demonstrate that incorporating gravity yields significantly better textures in seams—particularly in difficult areas like high contrast or motion blur—leading to markedly improved overall visual quality.

Chimera states are unique phenomena where an oscillatory system exhibits a simultaneous mix of synchronized and unsynchronized subsystems. Although numerous studies have explored various characteristics of chimeras, they typically rely on spatially correlated parameter heterogeneities that result in non-uniform spatial distributions. In this work, we theoretically and numerically investigate a two-population neural network governed by uniform spatially coupled parameter heterogeneities. We demonstrate that this approach yields novel chimera configurations, specifically patterns resembling standing and traveling waves.

Model-based reinforcement learning aims to approximate the optimal policy inherent within a simulated environment model to transfer those capabilities to a real environment through a specific mapping. While established techniques address this transfer, they often fail to produce policies robust against disturbances inherent in actual real-world implementation. This work introduces a novel robust control approach that utilizes a probabilistic model-based framework. By integrating a Gaussian Process Regression to model system dynamics with its uncertainty outputs, we implement Model Predictive Control (MTPC) to derive robust trajectories. Finally, this approach enables the direct optimization of a specific policy mapping for robustness. Experimental validation demonstrates the efficacy and robustness of the learned policies in achieving robust real-world execution.

In this paper, we introduce multi-layer quivers and demonstrate how they can model quasi-homogeneous quivers—also referred to as higher slice quivers—which were originally defined by Broomhead and Trepode in their study of higher slice algebras in the context of representation theory. We establish an equivalence category relating these two types of quivers. Leveraging a method previously developed by the authors in collaboration with Schiffler for constructing higher slice quivers, we now create a specific class of multi-layer quivers to facilitate the computation of their representation theories.

We examine the relationship between random tensor networks (RTNs) and reflected entropy by employing simple operations on these networks to construct corresponding reflected entropy calculations for a broad class of RTN configurations. We establish a direct link between the classical entanglement entropy of the dual network and reflected entropy. Consequently, this approach offers an explicit demonstration of the universal characteristic of reflected entropy found in random tensor networks where a dual structure exists.

Living systems utilize diverse physical and chemical mechanisms to generate and inherit data essential for their core functions. Although much literature details how diverse molecular switches store data across generations, this study introduces a different approach to heritability. We demonstrate that, within a broad class of stochastic systems, the long-term statistical properties of well-tuned, isolated dynamics yield Heritable information regarding diverse molecular switches. Our framework shows that a generic observer can access this information through two distinct mechanisms: first, by averaging over a long realization, and second, by averaging over many rapidly alternating copies of the system observed for short durations. Consequently, the statistical stability inherent in these systems facilitates robust data transmission without necessitating specialized structural components, such as distinct physical replications or(rplication) or transcriptional repression mechanisms.

Tunneling time constitutes a highly contentious issue in quantum physics, with recent research indicating that it can be defined by the shift in the spin of a particle's spinor axis, a concept known as the Larmor clock. In this study, we examine the behavior of a spin-1/2 particle's dynamics within a quantum system tunneling framework by employing a quantum tunneling time approach grounded in the quantum theory of the Larmor clock. We explore how spinor-nematic tensor components of the local spin density matrix correlate to determine their relevance. Findings indicate that the duration required for a spin-1/2 particle to traverse a rectangular potential barrier is the same as its time spent within the barrier region. We also note that it is crucial to examine the behavior of a system's spinor-nematic tensor components to accurately characterize the quantum tunneling time.

This study introduces a novel methodology for classifying galaxies into spiral and elliptical morphologies by leveraging the hyper-suprime-cam wide area survey data. By analyzing multiple imaging bands, this approach demonstrates that combining them significantly outperforms single-band observations. A machine-learned model, specifically a convolutional neural network, is trained to distinguish between these galaxy morphologies using stacked images created from the combined spectral data. The resulting classification system is benchmarked against established classifications derived from galaxy surface density and color gradients. The CNN model attains a classification accuracy exceeding 80\%, a figure notably higher than that achieved by traditional methods which reach 60\%-70\%. Both methods successfully identify the majority of early-type (elliptical) galaxies, though the traditional technique proves more effective at identifying late-type (spiral) galaxies. Finally, the study examines the relationship between the CNN-classified morphologies and specific host galaxy properties, including black hole mass ($M_{\rm BH}$), stellar mass ($M_{\rm *}$), and specific star formation rate ($\rm SSFR$) within an analysis sample of 1,000 active galactic nuclei hosted by $z<1$ galaxies.

The overwhelming majority of deep learning (DL) algorithms are designed under a fundamental constraint: they employ only real-valued optimization techniques, even though many input datasets are inherently complex-valued. This mismatch has driven significant recent research to address complex inputs within DL by focusing on complex weight architectures, which is the traditional approach for creating complex-friendly models. In this study, we propose an innovative alternative by introducing complex-valued hidden layers to achieve better feature extraction. We demonstrate that such a structure can be constructed using exclusively real-valization operations, thereby resolving the longstanding issue of complex-valued optimizations without requiring complex weight parameters. We name this methodology Co-domain Symmetry (CDs). CDs offers a streamlined framework for developing complex-valued DL models; it maintains compatibility with existing real-valued DL architectures and is without loss of generality. Comprehensive experimental results confirm that CDs models are capable of effectively and efficiently processing complex inputs, achieving superior performance compared to traditional complex-weighted counterparts and existing baseline methods.

This study tackles the issue of understanding how sensitive machine learning model predictions are to their training data. Since financial institutions increasingly employ AI and ML to automate decisions, minor shifts in the data can lead to drastic changes in outcomes, potentially harming customers. To address this, we created "RiskAI," a statistical toolbox that quantifies model sensitivity and and identify critical subpopulations. The tool combines a conceptually straightforward "local shift" approach with various techniques, including clustering and optimization, for comprehensive analysis. We tested RiskAI using two real-world datasets: one examining predictors of financial literacy and another examining risks associated with credit card default.

This work introduces the Scaled QUantum IDentifier (SQUID), an open-source framework designed for investigating hybrid Quantum-Classical algorithms in classification. Built on a classical PyTorch infrastructure, SQUID offers a streamlined pathway for developing custom quantum classifiers, facilitating easier experimentation with hybrid protocols. The framework supports specific features such as differentiable embedding layers, the capability to train variational models using stochastic gradient descent, and visualization tools for state evolution alongside loss and metric monitoring. Additionally, an implementation utilizing the PennyLane library enables hybrid quantum classical modeling. Extensive experiments were conducted on established Machine Learning benchmark datasets to demonstrate the framework's utility. Ultimately, this work anticipates that SQUID will significantly empower researchers exploring hybrid models by enhancing their capacity for creative exploration and iterative model refinement.

We investigate a two-particle active colloidal system confined within a two-dimensional channel and driven by Brownian motion, where each particle exerts equal but opposite propulsion forces. Our analysis focuses on the role of particle propulsion speeds, which govern both individual dynamics and collective behavior, specifically analyzing how an activity gradient influences the system across the full spectrum of particle and Brownian noise levels. Our findings demonstrate that even very small differences in driving speeds can induce substantial changes in the system's behavior, primarily mediated by the transition of particles from an anti-correlated state to a fully correlated state regarding their noise sources. We map these effects onto two key physical responses: the system's optical tunability, observable through changes in scattering patterns, and its rheological properties, observed via steady-state force responses. These phenomena are analyzed using physical reasoning and mathematical modeling based on the assumption of well-separated particles, validated against particle-based simulations which confirm the efficacy of this theoretical framework. Ultimately, we argue that active colloidal molecules represent a viable alternative to passive colloids, offering new possibilities for experiments in optical manipulation and the creation of active matter materials.

This paper investigates charge $e$ magnetorotons and edge excitations within fractional quantum Hall systems modeled by short-range interactions. Leveraging low-energy charge $e$ magnetorotons as low-lying excitations of the ground state, we establish rigorous lower bounds for the energy gaps of single-particle excitations. For circularly symmetric potentials, these magnetorotons are found to be non-degenerate in specific spin sectors. This constraint allows us to apply Kohn's sum rules to derive accurate estimates for both single-particle gaps and the spin excitation gaps. Furthermore, this method facilitates precise calculations of the charge and spin gaps even in scenarios where multiple magnetorotron sectors exist. Our findings indicate a significant divergence between the computed single-particle gaps and the gaps predicted by gap theory.

Epidemics spreading through social networks frequently follow a branching process where infections propagate from node to node. This transmission continues until the outbreak either subsides or encompasses the entire network, depending on the basic reproductive number ($R_0$). When outbreaks spread, they often form distinct clusters; this phenomenon is prevalent in networks where $R_0$ remains below a critical threshold. Our study proposes a geometric framework to analyze these clusters by applying stochastic growth models to their evolution. We demonstrate that network structures with high modularity—characterized by dense internal connections and sparse external ones—effectively suppress and localize spreading epidemics. Furthermore, we offer a geometric explanation for the density-dependent nature of historical outbreaks, such as the bubonic plague and cholera cases involving contaminated water supplies, where outbreaks were confined to areas with high population density but sparse infrastructure. These findings offer valuable lessons for the design of targeted disease prevention strategies.

In this study, we examine optimal parameters for cleaning point sources from wide-field, full-mission CMB datasets. We argue that standard Gaussian smoothing fails to prevent artifacts known as "X artifacts" near intense point sources. Instead, applying a multipole cutoff within the Maximum Likelihood estimator proves superior, ensuring no residuals remain. Using simulated CMB data, we confirm that this method significantly reduces artifacts from intense sources like Magellanic Clouds and stars. Additionally, our results suggest this approach is superior for integrating CMB data with non-CMB observations in the same sky region without generating interference.

Instructing an agent to execute a goal-oriented task using only natural language demands navigating referential ambiguity, where nouns may apply to multiple objects in an environment. This study addresses such ambiguity within 2D worlds containing multiple entities, where nomenclature is automatically assigned via graph convolutional neural networks analyzing the visual states. We evaluate three strategies for resolving this ambiguity during natural language-driven reinforcement learning: (1) modeling word frequencies assuming nouns refer to randomly selected objects with equal probability; (2) modeling frequent usage by assigning a uniform prior to objects only when encountering the object's name for the first time; (3) providing negative examples explicitly to the model when names are applied to objects not mentioned. Experiments conducted on the generalized gridworld environment demonstrate that these approaches substantially diminish the frequency of referential ambiguity compared to a baseline.

Shadow process tomography is an efficient technique for characterizing quantum processes that relies on sampling few randomly chosen measurements. In this study, we extend shadow process tomography to the characterization of completely asymmetric channel pairs through a teleportation-based approach. Since the success probability of standard teleportation protocol scales inversely with the square of the Hilbert space dimensions, our strategy involves decomposing the multi-dimensional channel into subspaces to circumvent this bottleneck. Specifically, we introduce a protocol that utilizes the smallest possible tensor factor as the "Alice" side in the role of the sender for channel teleportation. This optimization reduces the success probability scaling to a square-cubic relationship with the Hil space dimensions. When paired with shadow teleportation, standard shadow state tomography emerges as a special, low-dimensional instance.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer promising potential for diverse applications, ranging from remote sensing and imaging to cloud seeding and aerial data transmission. Addressing challenges such as limited battery life and flight duration constraints, this paper introduces a novel approach to expanding reach for short-time UAV deployments. This combination ensures the captured imagery remains sharp by minimizing defocus blur caused by altitude fluctuations. The interplay between molecular conformations and electronic transport mechanisms is established here through a study of the endohedral fullerenes Sc2TbN@C80 adsorbed on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate. Sc2TbTbN@C80 exhibits a change in molecular orientation upon exposure to the Ni substrate compared to a free molecule due to symmetry reduction. Transport measurements using a scanning tunneling microscope reveal that the conductance of the Sc2TbN@C80 molecule is temperature-dependent and exhibits a non-ohmic behavior, indicating a significant change in the dominant transport mechanism as the temperature rises. The Sc2TbTbN@C80 molecule undergoes a phase change from the alpha to the beta phase at approximately 100 Kelvin. DFT simulations further support these findings by showing that the conductance of the endo-fullerene molecule is highly dependent on the phase change in molecular symmetry.

The Internet of Things (IoT) involves networks of interconnected devices that communicate and exchange data, offering transformative capabilities for the future internet. These networks stand out due to data generation and collection from diverse sources, yet they struggle with resource scarcity, insecure data transmission, and limited scalability. Security remains a critical challenge, particularly as IoT devices generate sensitive information; however, most lack sufficient computing power for traditional security measures. This paper examines security needs within IoT networks and evaluates encryption algorithms suitable for low-power resource-constrained environments, ultimately recommending the best algorithm based on a comparative analysis of security and performance.

For spin qubits, Ramsey sequences constitute a fundamental measurement technique for estimating quantum state frequencies, enabling applications ranging from atomic clocks to quantum sensors. This work outlines a procedure for optimally configuring the phases and amplitudes of these Ramsey sequences. Within a sequential Bayesian experimental design, we determine each microwave pulse by utilizing the outcomes from prior pulses to refine state estimates and improve future performance. Numerical simulations indicate that this approach significantly enhances measurement precision. Ultimately, the proposed sequential strategy facilitates the efficient extraction of precise quantum state information.

Centrality metrics are essential for analyzing key nodes within networks. While existing centrality measures primarily rely on shortest path lengths, the recent introduction of centrality based on Gromov distance—a concept from metric geometry—offers a promising alternative. Defined as the minimal geodesic distance between two points on a metric space, this approach utilizes concepts from concepts geometry to account for distances on curved surfaces. Although successful in linking geometric properties with central network node importance, this method has limitations, as it lacks an upper bound for networks with specific geometries like hyperbolic forms. This study introduces Gromov centrality, which is adapted to remove such constraints. By eliminating the previous limitation, we enable its application to broader network types. Comparative analyses demonstrate that this new approach outperforms prior centrality measures regarding the node identification accuracy. These findings suggest that hyperbolic network centrality provides superior identification of important nodes compared to previous approaches.

This investigation explores the typical long-term dynamics of $k$-step maps defined on the real line within a family that possesses a unimodal (specifically, strongly monotone) structure, exhibiting a single smooth peak within a compact support domain. The analysis reveals a transition in prevalence: for low values of the control parameter, the system typically settles into a fixed point; increasing this parameter leads to a $k$-step period-doubling route toward chaos, where both periodic and aperiodic behaviors coexist. Crucially, unlike findings related to single-step monotone maps, our work establishes that smooth, strongly monotone $k$-step maps with odd $k$ possess a unique behavior: the non-trivial long-term activity (oscillatory or aperiodic modes) becomes increasingly prevalent as system parameters vary, while the non-oscillatory (convergent to an attractor) behavior becomes increasingly rare. This contrasts with even $k$ cases where such non-oscillatory behavior remains common.

Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a hybrid classical and quantum algorithm widely used for calculating the electronic states of molecules. A primary obstacle to its practical application lies in the high circuit complexity required for quantum subroutines, particularly those involving quantum excitation determination. To mitigate this, this study introduces a novel VQE approach called Qubit-Excitation-Based Adaptive VQE (QEB-VQE), which approximates quantum excitation operators using a basis of single-frozen excitation models. By incorporating a correlation correction term, the method ensures the accuracy of the ground state energy calculations across diverse molecular targets. We evaluated the QEB-VQE approach using two distinct ansatz states—Chemical Picture and Tailored ansatzes—and demonstrated that QEB-VQE yields results consistent with the full Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) ground state energies. However, the method proves most effective ansatzes perform optimally when these ansatzes are tailored specifically to molecular targets.

Deep generative models (DGMs) are increasingly popular for document generation tasks, yet their training remains difficult due to non-convex loss landscapes that hinder gradient-based optimization methods. This study investigates address this challenge by leveraging neural tensor models to estimate latent space representations directly from text, bypassing reliance on pre-trained models like GANs or VAEs. These representations feed into a generative decoder, creating a fully end-to-end architecture that facilitates more straightforward training. Experiments conducted on two datasets demonstrate that this approach yields state-of-the-art results in automated writing assessment, specifically on the Microsoft Research High School English Writing Challenge task. Additionally, the method achieves high-quality clustering in latent space that aligns well with human annotated assessments.

During inference, a cross-attention mechanism integrates this encoded representation with corresponding features from the cycle to guide unsupervised speech and audio synthesis, resulting in an efficient system that requires significantly less training data.

This capability addresses growing demands in data-intensive fields like biomedicine, a sector that generates substantial amounts of high-quality data from sources including electronic health records, medical imaging, and genomic sequencing. Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) represents a significant challenge within natural language processing, and numerous pre-trained models have been developed to address it. However, these models typically fall short in capturing the intricate, implicit sentiment cues present in input text. In this study, we introduce a new framework that applies Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SCP) to enhance implicit sentiment representation within ABCSA tasks. Our approach leverages sentiment cues from an intermediate Sentiment-aware Transformer to enrich a pre-trained language model (PLM) with ABSP-related knowledge. During SCP pre-training, we generate sentiment-embedded sentence pairs to construct supervised contrastive loss, enabling the model to distinguish the unique sentiment features of aspect sentences from those of neutral sentences. By training this enhanced PLM on an ABSO dataset, we achieve state-of-the-art results. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets confirm the effectiveness of our method.

This study investigates secure transmission strategies for Reflective Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted wireless systems, accounting for reciprocal hardware impairments (HIs) on both the Warden's and the UAV-User links. Employing a model that represents these HIs as additive Gaussian noise affecting transmitters, we determine both Secured Equivalent Total Transmit Power (SETTP) and SETTP-based Max-Min Rate (MM-SP) optimization models. These frameworks aim to simultaneously minimize the transmit power for a flying UAV and maximize the minimum of the SETTPs for ground users. To address this complexity, we propose efficient, suboptimal solutions. Specifically, we utilize the Majorization-Minimization (MM) algorithm to resolve the MM-SP formulation, while the SETTP model is addressed via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Comprehensive numerical simulations demonstrate the performance and validity of these approaches.

Executing any task inherently consumes these resources; however, we hypothesize that the deliberate investment in executive function enhances the effective value of those investments. To illustrate this concept and its implementation, we utilize a simplified simulation of an external environment that demands sequential task completion, where limited mental processing power restricts the number of internal processing steps available between interactions. Within this framework, each discrete mental step represents executive function; limited steps represent working memory capacity, and the choice of how many to deploy represents cognitive control, or executive control. While prior research suggests that learning to optimize this simulation with fixed step counts yields a useful cognitive agent, our approach expands this scope significantly more. HC-POL involves choosing a window of past states and rewards based on current state information, selecting which specific steps within that window are most valuable compared to others via a contrastive mechanism, and using this labeled set to update the policy. Utilizing the Sun Earth Connection Spectrograph aboard the Parker Solar Probe, this study presents the inaugural detection of solar wind spectral characteristics spanning 15 eV per particle to 20 MeV within the inner heliosphere, ranging from 29 to 90 solar radii. Although GPT-2 and similar large language models excel at generating coherent text, they currently lack the internal visual capabilities required to comprehend scenes depicted in images. Our analysis reveals that Random Walk and Parallel Tempering consistently outperform the other methods in most scenarios, whereas Parallel Tempering tends to yield superior results for cases characterized by complex contours. Furthermore, the study proposes a decision framework to assist users in selecting the most appropriate variant for specific applications.

Deep neural networks excel at achieving high accuracy within the confines of their training distribution, yet they frequently lack the ability to detect when this distribution has shifted during deployment. Addressing this critical issue in safety-critical domains necessitates integrating Distributionally Constrained Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection directly into training phases. Proposing a solution, this paper introduces a novel architecture called Distribution Gaussian Process Layers (DGPs). Unlike many current techniques that rely on a fixed, deterministic latent representation of input data distributions, DGPs model this representation as a Gaussian process to capture inherent uncertainty. Consequently, the framework provides a formal method for identifying data points that deviate significantly from the training distribution. The approach was evaluated against various synthetic benchmarks, where experimental findings confirm its ability to maintain top-tier in-distribution performance while maintaining robust in-context detection of distributional mismatches.

Periodically driven, isolated quantum systems typically evolve into an infinite-temperature thermal state over time; however, this dynamical thermalization is no longer expected when such systems are open and coupled to an environment. We investigate a weakly coupled, periodically driven quantum many-body system where the underlying weakly coupled system is a two-mode Bose-Hubbard model; due to its non-linear coupling with the surroundings, this open and driven configuration breaks the conventional balance between energy and phase, which would otherwise result in thermalization at infinite temperature. We find that under conditions of strong driving, the two bosonic modes can become decoupled, which results in one of the modes becoming "heated out of that state," leading to the emergence of Bose condensation in that scar-like state that would otherwise be a two-mode system. We find that the coupling strength between the two bosonic modes and the nature of that environment play crucial roles in determining whether this process leads to the decoupling that can generate such a unique dynamical state.

Time measurement relies on the counting of periodic phenomena. While historical timers, such as the Sun's diurnal cycle, exhibited statistical variations despite some periodicity, contemporary devices like atomic and electronic clocks operate with inherent, aperiodic fluctuations. To better understand the temporal characteristics of the noisy electronic and atomic "optical" clocks commonly used today, we investigated the time intervals between pulses from a single photon detector observing noisy optical light. Unlike previous studies that analyzed the frequency spectrum of chaotic light, our work evaluates its time-domain behavior using interval statistics. We observed two distinct regimes depending on the observation duration relative to the photodetection system's response time: at short delays relative to the response time, pulse arrival times follow exponential statistics; conversely, at long delays, they become uniformly distributed. This transition, occurring specifically when exceeding the inverse photodetection rate ($1/R$), is a novel phenomenon. In summary, our results demonstrate that the optical phase noise, previously studied via spectral analysis, manifests in the time domain as pulse arrivals governed by specific statistical rules determined by detector characteristics.

This paper presents a real-time service function chain (SFC) architecture designed for software-defined networking (SDN) with fog computing integration. A key challenge in deploying SFCs within fog environments is meeting strict latency requirements despite inherent network delays caused by virtualizing fog nodes locally. To address latency breaches and ensure service reliability, we introduce a joint optimization framework that manages network resources dynamically to maintain real-time performance. This approach also incorporates energy-efficient scheduling by integrating a renewable-powered fog node, thereby enhancing green computing capabilities. Evaluations across multiple scenarios demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing techniques in terms of reducing latency violations, improving reliability, and optimizing resource usage.

Loss functions are essential components in training deep neural networks. This research offers a fresh perspective by employing the concept of "gradient surgery," which involves temporarily pausing the backpropagation of specific losses to train only selected network parts. This method allows us to independently assess how losses influence separate network components. Our investigation, which included affine parameterization, Kullback-Leibler divergence, and cross-entropy, reveals that KL divergence hinders the learning of scale and shift parameters in the early stages, whereas cross-entropy succeeds where these parameters are learned effectively even with data augmentation techniques applied early.

This paper introduces a decentralized strategy for implementing Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) across integrated primary and secondary distribution systems. Building on a time-scale separation framework, the authors derive dynamic state-space representations for both primary and secondary network models. Optimal CVR is initially formulated as a centralized optimization problem, addressing dynamic, time-synchronized interactions between these systems. The formulation is then extended to a distributed framework leveraging network topologies to determine execution policies specific to networked transformers. Key findings indicate that execution policies rely solely on local state measurements and neighbor policy information. Notably, performance gaps between the distributed approach and the central optimal solution diminish as system scale increases. Simulation outcomes validate this methodology on a real-world test feed.

Dialogue-based text generation aims to create natural, open-domain conversations featuring rich information flow. While current solutions often rely on vast quantities of manually labeled data, supervised in supervised learning approaches frequently suffer from insufficient training diversity. This study introduces a new solution: a novel, fully automatic method designed solely to learn how to produce human-like dialogue responses. This work introduces a hybrid approach that integrates the joint modeling efficiency of energy-based functions with the alignment capabilities of generative models. By employing this framework in conjunction with in-context learning, we demonstrate a significantly enhanced performance across all benchmarks compared to current leading generative methods. Specifically, on MS MARCO MaxRet, the proposed model surpasses the baseline by +2.2, while achieving a maximum gain across all 11 evaluated benchmarks of up to +3.83.

The growing demand for precise and timely data in the fields of health, education, and social services has driven statistical data collection toward smaller geographic areas. However, in regions characterized by the collection of data over relatively small areas with a high variance in outcomes, traditional large-area models often fail to estimate outcomes accurately within each small region. This study evaluates the performance of a uniform large-area model, two variations of a hierarchical Bayesian small-area model, and two hybrid approaches combining these methods using survey outcome data from low- and middle-income countries. The analysis reveals that large-area models are particularly prone to overestimating or underestimating outcomes in the lowest- and highest-observed regions, whereas hierarchical Bayesian small-area models provide more accurate and precise inferences. Although large-area models prove more computationally efficient, hierarchical Bayesian small-area models are recommended for such contexts, as they yield superior accuracy and can be operationalized effectively through large, open-source tools like R.

This investigation explores gambling within the realm of a trader dealing with two noncommuting outcomes. A foundational equation is established linking the optimal betting ratio—derived from a specific optimal cumulative distribution function (CDF) for the payoff—to Shannon's capacity. The analysis reveals that while the Shannon equation remains valid across any single dimension, the optimal distribution function demonstrates continuity only within that particular dimension; in orthogonal dimensions, it assumes discrete states. Ultimately, these results suggest the practical implementation of optimal quantum betting strategies is most feasible within the context of discrete returns.

We conducted first-principles calculations to examine the quasiparticle band alignment and electronic characteristics of two-dimensional (2D) materials, specifically MA$_2$Z$_4$ (where M represents Mo, Ti, or W; A is Si or Ge; Z is N or P, or combinations thereof). Our findings confirm that the band alignment between the MA$_2$Z$_4$ monolayer and a 2D insulator substrate is consistently type-I, regardless of the constituent elements. Notably, we observed a stacking-independent second excitonic resonance peak in the optical absorption spectrum, a result validated by explicit calculations for both AB and BA stacking configurations. The presence of this peak signals strong coupling between the host material and the substrate. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that strain significantly impacts both the absolute energy levels of excitonic peaks and their relative ordering.

This numerical simulation models the creation of a protoplanetary disk resulting from the collapse of a prestellar core, utilizing smoothed-particle hydrodynamics coupled with a magnetic field and non-ideal MHD. An initial molecular cloud core consisting of 10,000 particles and 8 million Kelvin collapsed under its own gravity for approximately $1.5 \times 10^5$ years to form a central star of 0.5 solar masses and an associated disk. Despite magnetic braking preventing significant rotation of individual particles, the substantial angular momentum inherent within the core's overall rotation was funneled into collapsing material, adequately spinning up the infant disk. The simulation yielded a disk with a mass ratio to the star of 0.16, which is notably higher than the $\sim 0.01$ ratio typically observed in such systems. Consequently, the calculated disk mass of 80 Jupiter masses far exceeds the $\sim 1 M_J$ mass standard for protoplanetary disks, highlighting the need to implement a regulation mechanism for disk formation.

Differential atmospheric dispersion (DAD) remains a primary constraint for high-precision spectroscopy, particularly for instruments targeting shifts below 100 m s$^{-1}$. Although previous work has quantified DAD on-site, our recent study revealed site-to-site variations at the La Silla location. Investigating these discrepancies demands atmospheric modeling to assess sensitivity across different observing conditions. This study introduces new modeling methods developed on-site to characterize key atmospheric parameters. By measuring the magnitude of DAD at two opposite extreme wavelengths using a collimated laser beam, we derived vertical temperature profiles with high confidence. This approach allows for characterizing atmospheric parameters with uncertainties of approximately 1.5 K in temperature, 1.0 K in humidity, and roughly 1.0 m s$^{-1}$ optical air mass in the blue spectrum. Measurements were conducted over 100 vertical temperature profile measurements, the results align well with concurrent meteorological observations recorded within our own weather station.

This study addresses the challenge of predicting significant events within multi-temporal series, such as financial fluctuations, public opinion shifts, or biological pathways. The significant achievements driven by deep learning have introduced numerous ethical challenges, including algorithmic bias and threats to data privacy. To address these concerns, scholars employ techniques such as fairness evaluation, privacy preservation strategies, and federated learning to promote equity and protect data integrity. This study investigates how principles of fairness and privacy operate within federated learning environments. It evaluates the impact of two primary fairness definitions—individual fairness and statistical fairness—across multiple aggregation algorithms, including FedAvg, learning with noisy neighbors (NN), and more. Additionally, a novel algorithm termed FedQN-Path is introduced, combining noise injection within the FedAvg framework with a path-following optimization approach. This new method successfully enhances both individual fairness and the rate of convergence while maintaining better utility accuracy than competing methods. Finally, comprehensive simulations are presented to demonstrate the empirical performance of agnostic fairness and various privacy metrics under the proposed learning framework.

We examine the phenomenology of an extension within Supersymmetric Minimal $U(1)_X$ (USM$U(1)_X$) defined as $U(1)_X = T_{3R} + X$, which involves two additional $U(1)$-charged fields. In the USM$U(1)_X$ framework, right-handed neutrinos carry specific $U(1)_X$ quantum numbers, rendering this model attractive for radiative neutrino mass generation. We analyze a scenario where right-handed neutrino dark matter coexists with the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) stable due to $Z_2$ parity parity (R-particle). Results indicate that radiative neutrino mass generation coupled with these right-handed neutrinos can reproduce observed neutrino masses and mixing angles, consistent with current experimental data. We also examine neutral Higgs and chargino masses, noting they remain comparable to those in the MSSM. We further discuss how to differentiate this model from other $U(1)'$ extensions through searches for resonant production of the dark matter particle at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

Subsequently, this pre-trained model is applied to a system-specific dataset obtained from system simulations. Numerical evaluations confirm the effectiveness of this method, which demonstrates that unsupervised learning proves more efficient than supervised alternatives. Furthermore, the results highlight the superiority of this proposed unsupervised scheme compared to other supervised strategies.

We introduce a learning-based control technique designed to operate under data scarcity by leveraging side information. Specifically, drawing on the principles of the Prey-Predator paradigm in reinforcement learning, our approach enables the creation of "chasing" and "escaping" behaviors. We employ this technique to solve a sequence of locomotion challenges involving flying, swimming, and walking. By utilizing limited samples and training for just a single simulation step (1000 time units), the system generates chasing and evasive motion templates. These templates are then adapted to execute specific tasks. This method results in successful walking, flying, and swimming behaviors over large state spaces within the same learning phase. By requiring minimal interaction data and avoiding the need to explore difficult states, our data-driven strategy achieves effective and safe learning.

Toda conformal field theory represents a significant extension of Liouville theory, and within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3 Toda framework, we have developed a non-perturbative approach to construct form factors for the theory's local operators. We then expand our analysis within the operator algebra by examining composite operators formed through normal-ordered products. By utilizing the closed algebra of zero modes in Toda theories, we demonstrate that these constructed composite form factors maintain their closed algebra under our construction. Consequently, we apply this robust framework within a non-perturbative context to derive various $\mathfrak{sl}_3 Toda Toda$ Ward identities.

Although generative adversarial networks (GANs) have proven highly effective for high-resolution, realistic image generation, they often struggle with tasks requiring the preservation of object or part relationships. Specifically, approaches like pixel networks and those using region-based models fail to balance fidelity between regions adequately to maintain reliable relationships defined by natural language. Recent solutions address partial recovery to bridge this gap, exemplified by the Region GAN with Triplet loss (R-GAN), utilizing such metrics to restore regions partially based on natural language descriptions. However, R-GAN has been restricted to handling only single attributes like color, shape, or texture. To overcome this, we introduce FG-GAN, a framework combining FOGM (Feature Guided Object Matching) with GANs that supports recovering multiple simultaneous attributes. FG-GAN leverages a relation network within the triplet loss to determine which additional attributes are shared among the real reference image and the synthesized region pair. The model's loss function minimizes the discrepancy between real and synthetic regions while maximizing the agreement of non-common attributes. Empirical evaluations confirm FG-GN surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in multi-attribute recovery tasks.

Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) is a scalable variant of Fibre-based quantum key distribution that has recently demonstrated performance approaching that of standard Quantum Key Distributions. In this scalable TF-QKD approach, a phase-locked loop system is utilized, wherein the field phases of pulses transmitted by Alice and Bob are synchronized relative to one another. In response, we introduce a scalable TF-QKD method that eliminates the requirement for a phase-locked loop system, allowing Alice and Bob to send unpooled optical pulses through an optical fibre. This phase-unrelated scalable TF-KQ-K scheme matches the operational efficiency of the phase-locking approach while being far more scalable, making it the viable method for practical deployment.

Although object detection has made remarkable advancements, its capacity is limited to the specific categories and contexts encountered during training, classifying it as "closed-vocabulary." Conversely, if the target object or scene appears at test time without being present in training, open-vocabulary object detection aims to identify it accurately. This paper presents an efficient methodology to generate pseudo bounding-box labels, enabling models to be trained without requiring a significant increase in computational cost or data collection time. By introducing and training on these pseudo labels, the model effectively captures the characteristics and distributions of unseen objects and scenes. When deployed, the trained single-shot detector can reliably identify target objects in scenes vastly different from, yet related to, those seen during the initial data collection. Experiments across multiple benchmarks, including COCO-12.5K and OVSA, demonstrate a performance gain of 4.5% over current state-of-the-art methods.

This work details an investigation into the distribution of ionized gas, photodissociation region (PDR) gas, and atomic material surrounding the Class I protostar S1 within the Orion star-forming region. Utilizing data from both the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), we mapped ionized fluorine (FII) and FVII emission lines alongside the Hβ emission line. Analysis of these observations reveals that the FII emission originates from distances of roughly 1000-20,000 astronomical units (au) from S1, while Hβ arises from a more compact region extending to about 2000 au. Furthermore, we employed narrow-band HST imaging to detect CO and Pa$\alpha$ emissions. Combined with existing CO emission data and Pa$\alpha$ observations, our findings indicate that the atmosphere of S1 is surrounded by a complex structure consisting of a central PDR core overlaid by an outer ionized shell. These results offer significant insights into the mechanisms of mass accretion onto young stars and the regulation of outflows during the early stages of star and planet formation.

Neural architecture search (NAS) algorithms have become a cornerstone for discovering high-performance neural networks. Nevertheless, the substantial search space and the high costs associated with both design and validation present significant hurdles. Our study addresses validation costs by introducing parallel evaluation, enabling the assessment of numerous architectures simultaneously. Furthermore, the likelihood of search failure is often driven by suboptimal design choices or landscape interference, such as label smoothing. To validate that our methods remain robust against interference—even in complex scenarios with abundant label distributions across classes—we highlight a class imbalance case study. Our findings suggest that without proper handling, the search may erroneously identify inaccurate architectures due to interference.

This work introduces sum rules for the total and fractional energy deposited in one- and two-beam scattering contexts across various media. These relationships hold for every eigenchannel described by the Dissipative WKB method using Schrödinger-like equations. Derived from these rules, universal upper and lower limits for energy deposition in individual channels are established; notably, in scattering events involving two waves within a continuum medium using Open-Open boundary conditions, only the channel matching the incident wave's phase velocity can deposit energy. Furthermore, a specific case where one beam is a pump soliton interacting with a weak probe in a dispersive medium is examined. In scenarios with dual beams encountering a soliton, the sum rules also yield distinct spectral estimates for the resulting radiation channels.

Pruning techniques have recently been utilized to establish theories that explain various phenomena in deep neural networks, such as overparametrization and expressiveness. This research investigates these theories by examining pruning strategies that align with inherent network topologies—respectively handling intrinsic graph structures and weights—to determine if they can sift out unneeded features and redundant information to produce sparse configurations that maintain robust functionality. We observe two key outcomes: first, sparsifying Fully Connected Networks (FCNs) via intrinsic graph methods yields equivalent feature reduction as applying random pruning to standard convolutional architectures. Second, while integrating graph-based pruning into convolutional layers significantly surpasses random pruning in sparseness without harming performance, its ability to reduce features is outmatched by applying simple random pruning directly to fully connected layers. These findings indicate that intrinsic network topologies are effective at retaining functionality within a sparse framework but do not necessarily filter out redundant feature information. Furthermore, this suggests that convolutional layers are not inherently more efficient than fully connected ones at keeping essential features, and that fully connected networks can achieve the same predictive capabilities as convolutional networks once adjusted for an equivalent number of parameters.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a prevalent technique for embedding high-dimensional data, frequently utilized in machine learning for both visualization and feature extraction. However, because most existing methods are Euclidean in nature, they fail to account for data residing on a sphere. To address this, we propose VQMF-SNE, a versatile embedding approach for spherical data. Our method is founded on two main components: (1) constructing a connection between per-similarities within spherical spaces, and (2) implementing a constraint that keeps embedding points on the surface of the unit sphere. These elements are incorporated into a global objective function optimized using the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Furthermore, to mitigate issues with non-convex optimization, we present VQMF-SNE, a variational extension that relaxes point constraints into a smooth distribution. Experimental evaluations across multiple scenarios, alongside comparisons with various baselines, demonstrate that our approaches yield high-quality embeddings and offer enhanced performance over current state-of-the-art solutions.

Conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in image recognition, yet their performance often degrades with rotations; their translation invariance holds only within a specific range, and their ability to handle rotational variations remains limited. Within this paper, a novel approach is introduced that imparts full invariance to images against arbitrary rotations. Instead of relying on expensive data augmentation with rotated samples, the method achieves this by introducing a new class of convolutional kernels designed for intrinsic consistency with arbitrary rotational transformations. Although these orientation-dependent kernels are computationally more expensive—requiring $O(M^2)$ instead of $O(M)$ calculations for a kernel of size $M$—their total count remains constant throughout the network. Despite using only half the available training data compared to standard CNNs, an implementation of this orientation convolutional network achieved 80.8% accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset and 70.8% on the CIFAR-100 dataset, surpassing the accuracy of conventional CNNs.

This work examines how variations in light-quark and lepton masses affect the top quark's mass and its associated coupling to the Higgs boson. The analysis reveals that variations in lepton masses have a minimal effect on the pole mass and Yukawa coupling of the top quark. Conversely, the top mass shows a pronounced sensitivity to changes in down-type quark masses. This heightened dependence arises because the logarithm of the mass ratio, log(m_t/m_f), appears in the running of the SU(3) gauge coupling at one-loop order, which in turn impacts these quantities. The derived relationships are valuable because they facilitate constraints on the top mass's lower bounds based on experimental Higgs decay branching fractions involving bottom-antibottom pairs ($c\bar{c}, b\bar{b}$).

Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) serves as a prevalent imaging modality for identifying pulmonary diseases, including COVID-19. Although traditional capsule networks have demonstrated efficacy in object recognition, the growing demand for AI assistance in diagnosing this life-threatening virus necessitates a more robust solution. In this study, we present a novel two-stage time-distributed capsule network (TDTCN) that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in detecting the disease from LDCT scans without requiring image preprocessing or data augmentation. The model operates by first extracting medical images from the data, then classifying them as either infected or healthy. The proposed architecture consists of a convolutional layer followed by the attention mechanism within the residual capsule network. Utilizing a two-class dataset of 1,080 images (500 labeled COVID-19 cases and 580 labeled healthy patients), the trained model attained a remarkable accuracy rate exceeding 98.9%, establishing itself as a highly effective diagnostic tool.

This study introduces a comprehensive approach to generating low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite deployment configurations that adhere to predefined constraints. We introduce "spheres of exclusion" (Sox)—cylindrical safety zones around each satellite that we avoid during the placement of new objects. The proposed strategy is grounded in an optimized Markov chain Monte Carlo method, which is enhanced by a geometric tactic that efficiently positions new satellites within the remaining safe regions using a recursive algorithm. Furthermore, we describe post-placement techniques for calculating diverse sets of geometric and analytical parameters across various populations of SOX. These methods offer a robust means for studying self-organizing patterns in existing mega-constellations and explicitly mitigates risks related to collision density. As illustrative applications of these tools, we analyze existing LEO constellations to derive new insights regarding current spatial occupancy trends.

While dictionaries are abundant, they often fail to offer sufficient context for words. To address this, we introduce the LitMind Dictionary, an open-source dictionary designed to enrich dictionary entries with context-rich metadata. We augment a dataset of 10,000 words selected from the End-of-Year Dictionary with context metadata extracted from the Amazon Reviews dataset by representing it using a composite of word embeddings, such as Word2Vec and Gensim CC Vectors. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we employ LongShort-Term (LSTL-S), LSTL-SV, and LongShort-Term (LSTL-SV) algorithms to generate the context for each word. We then use these contexts to create a new task called "Contextual Word Matching" and show how LSTL-S can be trained using LSTL-S to create the context for each word.

Explainable recommendation systems have garnered significant attention recently due to their ability to enhance system interpretability, user trust, and transparency. Among various methods, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Attribution (LIME) stands out by generating explanations without relying on the underlying algorithm. However, we have uncovered critical shortcomings in LIME-generated explanations for recommendation systems, including low adherence and inconsistency. Specifically, low adherence means items marked as irrelevant by the model are sometimes included in the final explanations. Furthermore, we demonstrated that LIME is sensitive to its weighting function: the inclusion or exclusion of specific items depends on the chosen parameter values rather than the data itself. Additionally, we demonstrated that item inclusion in the top-k list is unstable; a slight alteration in the weight function can flip an item from being included to excluded. To address these limitations, we propose AdherenceRS (ARS), a novel method for generating explanations for item recommendations. Empirical evaluations on two established datasets show ARS attains significantly higher adherence than LIME. Furthermore, ARS demonstrates superior adherence and stability across all experimental conditions when compared to three baseline approaches. Detailed results regarding ARS's adherence and stability are presented.

Semiconductor surfaces typically suffer from interface states that pin the carrier Fermi level near mid-gap, rendering both bulk and near-surface regions unsuitable for near-threshold electronic applications. To overcome this limitation and enable bulk materials like InAs near the surface to access regimes below band-edge thresholds, we propose extending in situ chemical etching of InAs quantum wells within Si/Moiré structures all the way to completion of the substrate etching. Our results indicate that this approach effectively eliminates Fermi level pinning near the interface. Additionally, this and similar strategies could benefit other III-IV semiconductor heterostructures such as InGaAs on Si.

High-energy X-ray and ultraviolet (UV) radiation significantly impacts exoplanets orbiting active stars, potentially stripping atmospheres and driving atmospheric chemistry. The young AU Mic system hosts two planets similar in mass to Neptune, providing a unique opportunity to evaluate these stellar-planet interactions through both planetary modeling and direct observation. This study reports on FUV observations collected simultaneously with X-ray data during quiescence and multiple flares at AU Mic. These findings indicate that the star's FUV emission levels match expectations derived from its luminosity curve, particularly regarding the planet AU Mic b. Furthermore, during two flares captured in X-rays, we detected corresponding FUV flares. The magnitude of these FUV flares aligns well with the observed X-ray events when scaled by X-ray luminosity, although the FUV flare amplitude during one of these events exceeded previous superflare records made of the star. Consequently, these superflare events suggest that AU Mic b and c could experience substantial atmospheric loss over their estimated 10 Myr system age due both to transient flares and sustained quiescence emission.

Reactions to radiation friction within a medium are analyzed under the assumption that inclusive measurements exist. The determination of the force acting on an excited quark in such media proves nontrivial; specifically, the number of photons detected with specific momentum in the radiation spectrum provides only an upper limit on the magnitude of the quark's acceleration, as evidenced by the inclusion matrix element inequality of $dN_\gamma/dk \leq (dN_\gamma/dk)_{max} \propto a^2/k$. This constraint arises because any single measurement probes only a narrow subset of phase space, whereas the total number of photons encompasses the entire phase space. Assuming radiation occurs in a quasi-adiabatic regime where the medium resists acceleration, we derived an expression for resistive force based on these considerations.

In classification tasks involving imbalanced data sets, the standard nearest neighbor (NN) method is often inadequate for achieving satisfactory performance. This paper proposes a statistical technique for constructing classification rules specifically tailored to such imbalanced scenarios. By incorporating the proportion of majority and minority classes directly into the decision rule, this approach explicitly addresses class disparity, a factor typically overlooked in conventional NN methods. Consequently, theoretical analysis demonstrates that this modified rule is consistent, thereby converging on the optimal Bayes classifier as the number of samples tends toward infinity. Furthermore, empirical evaluations using simulations and real-world data comparisons reveal that this statistical NN approach significantly outperforms traditional nearest neighbor algorithms in classifying imbalanced datasets.
